v0.20.0 — a new chain, wallets that protect people, a network that heals itself

**This release starts a new chain.** Every operator has to update, and move their old chain data
aside. Forget that, and the new build refuses to start on the old database and names the rename —
it neither overwrites the old chain nor runs on it. Balances and stakes of the old chain do not
carry over.

**Operators: how to update**

1. Stop your node.
2. In its data directory, rename — do not delete — `helix-data.redb` and `helix-peers.txt`
   (for example to `helix-data.redb.pre-0.20.0`). **Keep `validator-key.json` and
   `validator-key.signing-state.json` where they are**: the key is your validator, and the
   signing state knows it belongs to the old chain and starts over on the new one by itself.
   In the desktop wallet, **Validate → Reset local chain** does this for you.
3. Install 0.20.0 and start the node. It joins the chain with genesis
   `<GENESIS_HASH — fill in after the reset>`, which is compiled in.
4. Wait until `helix chain status` (or `GET /status`) shows `peer_count` above zero and the height
   moving. Only then stake — a validator that is not connected cannot vote once it is active.
5. **Open your P2P port (8546 by default)** if you can. The node finds its own address and
   announces it; every validator that can be reached directly takes load off the one everyone
   reaches today, and the network no longer stops when that one's link drops.

If you set these before, change them now:

- **`HELIX_REWARD_ADDRESS` is no longer read.** It only ever worked for a validator alone on its
  chain. The reward address is now on-chain: `helix tx set-reward-address <address>` (or in the
  desktop wallet, on your validator card). Only your own share and commission go there — your
  delegators keep theirs. The node tells you at start if the old setting is still present.
- **`HELIX_KEEP_BLOCKS` and `HELIX_KEEP_BYTES` are read strictly.** A value the node cannot read
  (`500_000`, `1.5G`) used to be taken for "no limit" — now the node does not start and says how
  to write it. `HELIX_KEEP_BYTES` accepts `120G`, `120GiB` and `120 GB` alike (all binary).
- **`HELIX_P2P_SEED_PEERS` and `HELIX_P2P_PUBLIC_ADDR` are checked.** A seed written as
  `203.0.113.7:8546` used to be skipped without a word; now the node does not start and names the
  multiaddr it meant (`/ip4/203.0.113.7/tcp/8546`). The same for an announced address no peer
  could dial.
- **`HELIX_TRUSTED_CHECKPOINT` takes three parts now:** `<height>:<block hash>:<state root>`, as
  `GET /sync/checkpoint` prints it. A two-part checkpoint still anchors the blocks but no longer
  licenses the snapshot shortcut — the node says so and syncs from genesis instead. **A value the
  node cannot read stops it**, and says what is wrong ("the block hash has 63 characters, and a
  block hash has 64"): ignoring it meant replaying the whole chain onto a disk that may not hold it.

Disks:

- **`HELIX_KEEP_BLOCKS` and `HELIX_KEEP_BYTES` now apply while the node catches up.** A node
  joining from block 0 used to write the whole chain before its window did anything.
- **Below 1 GiB free on the disk that holds the chain database, the node stops writing and exits**
  with a message that says so — and keeps exiting on restart until there is room. A write that runs
  out of space half-way leaves a database no build can open; stopping first keeps it intact.
  (Linux and macOS; Windows cannot report free space this way.)

**Command line: passphrases are never typed on the command line**

- `--passphrase` takes no value any more: it asks, twice, without echo. `--passphrase <value>` is
  refused with an explanation — treat such a passphrase as exposed.
- Scripts use `--passphrase-file <path>` — now on **every command that signs**, not only when a
  wallet is created, so an automated wallet no longer has to be kept in plaintext.
- `wallet encrypt` asks instead of taking the passphrase as an argument; `--remove` removes it.
- `wallet new` never overwrites an existing wallet file, and key files are written readable by
  their owner only.
- A fee the wallet priced itself is capped at 1 HLX: a node that lies about the base fee can no
  longer have your wallet sign away your balance as a fee.

**Desktop wallet**

- Locks itself after 10 minutes without use — the key is cleared from memory, and a laptop closed
  with the wallet open wakes up locked.
- A passphrase can be set or changed later, under Settings → Passphrase.
- A validator can choose where its rewards go, on its validator card.
- A wallet file whose address does not belong to its key does not open.
- The same 1-HLX fee ceiling as the command line.
- Fees are priced on what the block carries: after an account's first transaction a block no
  longer carries its public key, so the wallet stops paying for it — about a third less per
  transfer. The command line does the same.
- Its node keeps about 4 GB of recent history instead of every block — on a laptop the full chain
  grows by ~1.7 GB a day. Your own `HELIX_KEEP_BYTES`/`HELIX_KEEP_BLOCKS` still win.
- If its node refuses the chain stored on your machine — after this reset, for one — the wallet
  says so and opens the reset, instead of leaving an exit code at the bottom of the console.

**Network**

- A node whose connection died on one side only can send again — before, it could stay connected
  and mute for an hour, and the chain stopped with it.
- A node with fewer than three peers looks for more, instead of waiting until it has none.
- A validator that restarts misses at most its first turn, instead of sitting out two minutes of
  its own rounds.
- Transactions travel on a gossip lane of their own: a vote no longer waits in the same queue as a
  flood of them.
- Blocks cross the network compact: the header and the ids of the transactions, which every node
  rebuilds from the transactions it already holds. A full block of ~1.4 MB crosses a link as
  ~15 KB; a node that is missing a transaction fetches the whole block instead of guessing.
  `/diagnostics` counts both (`compact_blocks_rebuilt`, `compact_blocks_not_rebuilt`).
- A node forwards only what it has read and accepted — garbage sent to one node no longer gets
  its honest neighbours banned.
- A proposer no longer packs transactions a block cannot apply, and none of them get lost.
- Block batches are streamed and large answers queued: a stranger asking for blocks no longer
  drives a node's memory up. A submitted transaction's signature is checked before the pool's
  lock, so a flood of submissions cannot hold up the next block.
- Answering another node's request for blocks no longer holds up this node's own votes, and an
  answer never exceeds what the asker can read — a node that fell behind during a busy stretch
  can catch up again over the network.
- The health line in the log no longer tells an operator that a restart cannot help — it says
  only what the node can actually know.
- A node that is not an active validator — not staked, or staked and not yet active — says so once
  in its log, instead of a warning every two seconds. A validator alone on its chain no longer
  warns twice a block that its round cannot finish.
- A node syncing from another node's RPC checks that each batch builds on the state it holds.
  Where it does not, the node applies nothing and names the possible causes, instead of syncing to
  the tip on a state that is not the chain's.

**Why a new chain: rules that changed**

- The chain starts with 100,000 HLX issued — the bootstrap validator's 10,000 stake and 90,000
  liquid, out of which the operators are funded — down from 510,000.

- Validators are jailed for a *rate* of missed blocks, not only a run of them: a validator that
  signs one block in thirteen no longer counts as present.
- A single double-sign can be punished once, not over and over with the same evidence.
- Stake that arrives after a governance proposal now counts in its quorum as well as in its
  votes — a latecomer with 44 % of the stake could carry a two-thirds vote before.
- A governance proposal leaves the chain state once its voting period is over, passed or not; what
  it changed stays in force, and the proposal stays on the chain as its transaction.
- Opening a governance proposal takes the chain's minimum validator stake — whatever governance has
  set it to at the time — instead of any stake at all. Voting still takes any stake.
- A guardian who keeps re-approving can be removed by the owner; delegated stake that moves away
  from a validator stays slashable for it during the redelegation window.
- A `.hlx` name has a price, burned on registration: 5 HLX for five characters or more, 50 HLX for
  four, 500 HLX for three — names used to cost only the transaction fee, so every short name could
  be held for a few fees. An address holds one name; registering another releases the first. The
  command line asks `--accept-price` for short names; the desktop wallet shows the price on the
  button; apps get it from `name_registration_price_nano` or from `GET /names/:name` (404 with
  `registration_price_nano`).
- In a social recovery each guardian holds one vote: approving another key moves that guardian's
  vote and leaves the others' standing, where it used to restart the whole request.
  `GET /accounts/:address/recovery` lists every named key (`pending_keys`).
- A joining node accepts an unstaked producer only for the genesis validator, and a snapshot only
  against a state root the operator supplied.
- A transaction from an address the chain has seen before is kept in blocks **without** its public
  key — about a third of every transfer. The chain records each key the first time it is used.
  Wallets need no change: they keep sending the key, and the transaction id they are given is the
  one the block carries. Anyone who computes a transaction id or checks a Merkle proof themselves
  should read the transaction format in `docs/reference.md`: the id no longer covers the key, and
  a proof starts from the new `leaf_hash`.
